exam: LFCS (Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator), performance-based, 2 h, pass 67%
domains_note: Verify current domains and weights at https://training.linuxfoundation.org/certification/linux-foundation-certified-sysadmin-lfcs/ before booking. Commonly listed: Operations & Deployment, Networking, Storage, Essential Commands, Users & Groups.
source: Re-chunked from docs/plan/calendar/day-01..04 (home Course 1) into 5-minute micro-challenges. Break-and-fix versions run at home (Incus lab) or on a local lab once one exists.

env_legend.host-tmp: own processes and files under a mktemp dir on this machine; no sudo
env_legend.docker: docker run --rm only; never touches anything else
env_legend.systemd-user: transient `systemd-run --user` units that vanish afterwards; no system units, no sudo

items.title: Walk a process through S → T → S → gone
items.task: Start `sleep 1000 &`. Predict the `ps -o stat= -p $PID` letter after each of: start, `kill -STOP`, `kill -CONT`, `kill -TERM`. Then predict `wait $PID; echo $?`. Run it and compare.

items.title: Predict 126, 127, 130, 137, 143
items.task: Before pressing Enter, write down the exit code each prints: `bash -c 'exit 3'`; a file without the exec bit run as ./file; `nosuchcommand`; `sleep 100 & kill -9 $!; wait $!`; `sleep 100 & kill $!; wait $!`. Explain the 128+n rule in one sentence.

items.title: The signal you can't trap
items.task: Write a 5-line bash script that traps TERM (clean exit with a message) and INT (ignore). Prove both from a second shell. Then send the one signal that skips your cleanup. Which two signals can never be caught, and why does that matter for a pod's preStop?

items.title: Make a zombie, then make it disappear without killing it
items.task: Create a zombie on purpose (hint-free: a parent that never waits). Show it with ps (STAT Z). Try `kill -9` on the zombie and predict the result. Then remove it the correct way and explain who reaps it.

items.title: Why does docker stop take 10 seconds?
items.task: Using only `docker run --rm -d` with ubuntu: time `docker stop` for `sleep 600` with and without `--init`, and read each exit code (`docker inspect` before removal, or run without --rm). Predict both times and both codes first.

items.title: for f in $(ls) lies
items.task: In a temp dir, create `a b.log` and `c.log`. Predict how many lines `for f in $(ls *.log); do echo "[$f]"; done` prints, then fix it without ls. Bonus: make the broken version safe with IFS and explain why that's still worse.

items.title: free vs available
items.task: Predict which number is bigger on this machine: MemFree or MemAvailable, and by roughly how much. Check with `grep -E 'MemFree|MemAvailable|^Cached|Buffers' /proc/meminfo`. Explain in one sentence what's in the gap and why 'low free memory' alerts are usually wrong.

items.title: Who does the OOM killer pick?
items.task: Start two of your own processes: one small, one that allocates ~200 MB (e.g. `python3 -c 'b=bytearray(200*2**20); input()'`). Predict which has the higher `/proc/<pid>/oom_score`, then check it. Change one with `echo 500 > /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj` (allowed for your own process) and re-predict. Link it to Kubernetes QoS classes in one sentence.

items.title: df says full, du says empty
items.task: In a mktemp dir: write a 100 MB file, keep it open (`exec 3<bigfile` in a subshell or `sleep 1000 < bigfile &`), then delete it. Predict what `du -sh .`, `ls`, and `lsof +L1 | grep bigfile` show. Free the space without restarting anything else.

items.title: What does x mean on a directory?
items.task: In `docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash` as a non-root user (useradd + su): create dir d with a file inside. Predict what `ls d` and `cat d/file` do with modes 0644 and 0711 and 0755 on d. Test all three.

items.title: Restart= on-failure vs always vs on-abnormal
items.task: Run `systemd-run --user --unit=upskill-demo -p Restart=on-failure -p RestartSec=1 sh -c 'sleep 2; exit 1'`. Predict how many restarts you see in 10 s (`journalctl --user -u upskill-demo`), then repeat with `exit 0`, and with Restart=always. Stop it with `systemctl --user stop upskill-demo`. Which policy would restart after a SIGKILL from the OOM killer?

items.title: ulimit in your shell lies about your service
items.task: Predict the output of `ulimit -n` in your shell vs `systemd-run --user --wait --pipe -p LimitNOFILE=64 sh -c 'ulimit -n'`. Explain why setting ulimit in a login shell never fixes 'too many open files' in a service, and where you'd set it instead (drop-in path).
